name: Andromeda
description:
In Greek myth, Andromeda was a princess chained to a sea rock as an offering to the monster Cetus, until Perseus rescued her.

Its brightest star is Alpheratz, which also marks a corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. Mirach is close behind.

Andromeda is best seen on autumn evenings, high overhead in October and November.

Fun fact: the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away, is the most distant thing most people can see with the naked eye.

name: Antlia
description:
Antlia, the Air Pump, has no myth. French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille named it in the 1750s to honour the air pump, an exciting new scientific instrument at the time.

It's faint: its brightest star, Alpha Antliae, is only about magnitude 4.3.

From southern Canada it sits low in the south on April evenings. From farther north it barely clears the horizon.

Fun fact: Lacaille named 14 southern constellations, most of them after scientific instruments and tools.

name: Apus
description:
Apus, the Bird of Paradise, was created by Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s, inspired by the brilliant birds of New Guinea.

Its brightest star, Alpha Apodis, is an orange giant of about magnitude 3.8.

Apus lies close to the south celestial pole, so it never rises from Canada. You'd need to travel to the Southern Hemisphere to see it.

Fun fact: its name comes from the Greek for "no feet", because the first bird of paradise skins to reach Europe had their feet removed.

name: Aquarius
description:
Aquarius, the Water Bearer, is often linked to Ganymede, the youth Zeus carried to Olympus to pour drinks for the gods. It's one of the oldest named constellations.

Its brightest stars are Sadalsuud and Sadalmelik, both yellow supergiants near magnitude 3.

Aquarius is best seen low in the south on autumn evenings, in September and October.

Fun fact: the Eta Aquariid meteor shower, made of dust from Halley's Comet, radiates from Aquarius each May.

name: Aquila
description:
Aquila, the Eagle, carried Zeus's thunderbolts in Greek myth, and in some stories snatched Ganymede up to Olympus.

Its brightest star, Altair, is one of the closest bright stars at about 17 light-years. It forms one corner of the Summer Triangle with Vega and Deneb.

Aquila is best seen on summer evenings, high in the south from July to September.

Fun fact: Altair spins so fast, about once every nine hours, that it bulges noticeably at its equator.

name: Ara
description:
Ara, the Altar, is where the Greek gods swore loyalty to each other before their war against the Titans. The Milky Way above it was imagined as the altar's smoke.

Its brightest star, Beta Arae, is an orange supergiant near magnitude 2.8.

Ara lies far south, so it stays hidden below the horizon from Canada.

Fun fact: the Sun-like star Mu Arae has at least four known planets.

name: Aries
description:
Aries, the Ram, is the golden-fleeced ram of Greek myth that rescued Phrixus and Helle. Its fleece later became the prize sought by Jason and the Argonauts.

Its brightest stars are Hamal, an orange giant, and Sheratan.

Aries is best seen on late autumn and early winter evenings, from November to January.

Fun fact: about 2,000 years ago the Sun was in Aries at the March equinox, so that spot is still called the "First Point of Aries", even though it has since drifted into Pisces.

name: Auriga
description:
Auriga, the Charioteer, is often identified with Erichthonius, a legendary king of Athens said to have invented the four-horse chariot. He's pictured carrying a goat and her kids.

Its brightest star, Capella, is the sixth brightest star in the night sky and is really a system of four stars.

Auriga is best seen on winter evenings, nearly overhead in January and February. From most of Canada, Capella never sets.

Fun fact: the Milky Way runs through Auriga, which holds three bright star clusters, M36, M37 and M38.

name: Boötes
description:
Boötes, the Herdsman, is said to drive the bears of Ursa Major around the pole. One story makes him Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto.

Its brightest star, Arcturus, is an orange giant and the brightest star in the northern half of the sky. Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle to find it: "arc to Arcturus".

Boötes is best seen on late spring and summer evenings, from May to July.

Fun fact: light from Arcturus was used to switch on the lights of the 1933 Chicago World's Fair.

name: Caelum
description:
Caelum, the Chisel, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s after the engraver's chisel, one of many tools he placed in the southern sky.

It's very faint: its brightest star, Alpha Caeli, is only about magnitude 4.4.

From southern Canada it rises just above the southern horizon on January evenings, below Orion and Lepus. It's hard to spot from farther north.

Fun fact: Caelum is one of the smallest constellations, the eighth smallest of the 88.

name: Camelopardalis
description:
Camelopardalis, the Giraffe, has no ancient myth. Petrus Plancius introduced it around 1612 to fill a dim, empty region near the north celestial pole. Its name is Greek for "camel-leopard", an old word for a giraffe.

Its stars are faint; the brightest, Beta Camelopardalis, is only about magnitude 4.

It's circumpolar from Canada, so it's up all year, and highest on winter evenings.

Fun fact: despite being so faint, it's the 18th largest constellation.

name: Cancer
description:
Cancer, the Crab, was sent by Hera to distract Heracles while he fought the Hydra. Heracles crushed it, and Hera placed it in the sky.

It's the faintest zodiac constellation. Its brightest star, Al Tarf, is only about magnitude 3.5.

Cancer is best seen on late winter and spring evenings, in March and April.

Fun fact: at its centre is the Beehive Cluster (M44), a swarm of stars visible to the naked eye under dark skies.

name: Canes Venatici
description:
Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs, are the dogs Boötes the Herdsman holds on a leash as he chases the bears around the pole. Johannes Hevelius created it in the 1680s.

Its brightest star is Cor Caroli, "Charles's Heart", named in honour of King Charles I of England.

It's best seen on spring evenings, high overhead in April and May.

Fun fact: it holds the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51), the first galaxy in which spiral arms were seen, by Lord Rosse in 1845.

name: Canis Major
description:
Canis Major, the Great Dog, is one of Orion's hunting dogs, following him across the sky. Some stories make it Laelaps, a dog so fast nothing could escape it.

Its brightest star, Sirius, is the brightest star in the night sky, just 8.6 light-years away.

Canis Major is best seen on winter evenings, low in the south in January and February.

Fun fact: the "dog days" of summer are named after Sirius, which the ancient Greeks saw rising with the Sun in the hottest part of the year.

name: Canis Minor
description:
Canis Minor, the Little Dog, is Orion's second hunting dog. It's small, with only two easily seen stars.

Its brightest star, Procyon, is the eighth brightest star in the sky and one of the closest, about 11.5 light-years away. It forms the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse.

Canis Minor is best seen on winter evenings, from January to March.

Fun fact: Procyon's name means "before the dog", because it rises just before Sirius, the Dog Star.

name: Capricornus
description:
Capricornus, the Sea-Goat, is a goat with a fish's tail. In Greek myth it's often linked to the god Pan, who turned partly into a fish to escape the monster Typhon.

Its brightest star, Deneb Algedi, marks the goat's tail. Algedi, at the head, is a double star that sharp eyes can split.

Capricornus is best seen low in the south on late summer and early autumn evenings, in August and September.

Fun fact: the Tropic of Capricorn is named after it, because the Sun was in Capricornus at the December solstice when the name was given.

name: Carina
description:
Carina, the Keel, was once part of Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts. Lacaille split the giant ship into three constellations in the 1750s.

Its brightest star, Canopus, is the second brightest star in the night sky.

Carina lies far south and stays hidden from Canada. Canopus can only be seen from about latitude 37° N or farther south.

Fun fact: Carina holds Eta Carinae, a massive, unstable star that briefly became one of the brightest in the sky in the 1840s.

name: Cassiopeia
description:
Cassiopeia was a vain queen of Ethiopia who boasted she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs. As punishment, Poseidon placed her in the sky on her throne, where she spends half the night upside down.

Its five brightest stars form a W or M shape. Schedar and Caph are the brightest.

Cassiopeia is circumpolar from Canada, so it's up every night of the year. It's highest on autumn evenings.

Fun fact: in 1572, Tycho Brahe saw a supernova here, proving that the heavens could change.

name: Centaurus
description:
Centaurus, the Centaur, is often identified with Chiron, the wise centaur who taught heroes such as Achilles and Jason.

Its brightest star, Alpha Centauri, is the closest star system to the Sun at about 4.4 light-years. Its faint companion, Proxima Centauri, is the nearest single star.

From southern Canada, only the centaur's northern stars rise low in the south on May evenings. Alpha Centauri itself never rises here.

Fun fact: Centaurus holds Omega Centauri, the largest and brightest globular cluster in our galaxy.

name: Cepheus
description:
Cepheus was the king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. He sits beside his queen near the north celestial pole.

Its stars form a shape like a simple house. Its brightest star is Alderamin. Mu Cephei, the "Garnet Star", is one of the reddest stars visible to the naked eye.

Cepheus is circumpolar from Canada, visible all year, and highest on autumn evenings.

Fun fact: Delta Cephei gave its name to Cepheid variables, pulsating stars astronomers use to measure distances to other galaxies.

name: Cetus
description:
Cetus, the Sea Monster, was sent by Poseidon to ravage Ethiopia after Queen Cassiopeia's boast. Perseus killed it before it could devour Andromeda.

Its brightest star is Diphda, also called Deneb Kaitos. Menkar marks the monster's head.

Cetus is best seen on autumn evenings, in the south in November and December.

Fun fact: the star Mira, "the Wonderful", brightens and fades over about 11 months, from easily visible to too faint to see without a telescope.

name: Chamaeleon
description:
Chamaeleon, named after the lizard that changes colour, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s from their voyages to the East Indies.

It's small and faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Chamaeleontis, is only about magnitude 4.1.

Chamaeleon lies close to the south celestial pole, so it never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: the Chamaeleon dark clouds, about 500 light-years away, are one of the nearest places where new stars are forming.

name: Circinus
description:
Circinus, the Compass, is a drawing compass, not a navigator's. Lacaille named it in the 1750s, placing it beside Norma, the carpenter's square.

It's small. Its brightest star, Alpha Circini, is about magnitude 3.2.

Circinus lies far south and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: the Circinus Galaxy, one of the closest active galaxies, hides behind the Milky Way's dust here and wasn't discovered until 1977.

name: Columba
description:
Columba, the Dove, is usually said to be the dove Noah released from the ark to find dry land. Petrus Plancius introduced it in the 1590s.

Its brightest star is Phact, about magnitude 2.6.

From southern Canada it sits low in the south on January and February evenings, below Lepus and Canis Major. From farther north it barely rises.

Fun fact: Mu Columbae is a "runaway star", flung out of the Orion region about 2.5 million years ago and still racing away.

name: Coma Berenices
description:
Coma Berenices, Berenice's Hair, honours Queen Berenice II of Egypt. She cut off her long hair as an offering for her husband's safe return from war. When it vanished from the temple, it was said to have been placed among the stars.

Its stars are faint; the brightest is Beta Comae Berenices, a Sun-like star.

It's best seen on spring evenings, high in April and May.

Fun fact: beyond its stars lies the Coma Cluster, which holds over a thousand galaxies.

name: Corona Austrina
description:
Corona Austrina, also called Corona Australis or the Southern Crown, is a small arc of stars the ancient Greeks saw as a wreath. One story says Dionysus placed it in the sky in honour of his mother, Semele.

Its brightest stars are only about magnitude 4.

From southern Canada it barely clears the southern horizon on July and August evenings, below Sagittarius. From farther north it stays hidden.

Fun fact: it holds one of the nearest star-forming regions, the Corona Australis cloud, about 430 light-years away.

name: Corona Borealis
description:
Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown, is the crown Dionysus gave to Ariadne when they married. He later threw it into the sky.

Its brightest star is Alphecca, the jewel of the crown. Its stars form a neat semicircle.

It's best seen on early summer evenings, in June and July, between Arcturus and Vega.

Fun fact: T Coronae Borealis, the "Blaze Star", is a recurring nova that flares up roughly every 80 years, after outbursts in 1866 and 1946.

name: Corvus
description:
Corvus, the Crow, was Apollo's bird. Sent to fetch water, it stopped to eat figs and blamed a water snake for the delay. Apollo saw through the lie and placed the crow, the cup and the snake in the sky, with the crow forever kept from drinking.

Its four brightest stars form a small quadrilateral. The brightest is Gienah.

Corvus is best seen low in the south on spring evenings, in April and May.

Fun fact: it holds the Antennae Galaxies, a pair of colliding galaxies.

name: Crater
description:
Crater, the Cup, is Apollo's cup from the same story as Corvus: the crow was sent to fill it with water but stopped to eat figs instead.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Delta Crateris, is about magnitude 3.6.

Crater is best seen low in the south on spring evenings, in April.

Fun fact: in the sky, the cup sits on the back of Hydra, the water snake, right next to Corvus.

name: Crux
description:
Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest of the 88 constellations. Its four bright stars form a cross that has guided navigators in the Southern Hemisphere for centuries.

Its brightest star is Acrux, a multiple star system. Mimosa is the next brightest.

Crux never rises from Canada. You'd need to be south of about latitude 27° N to see all of it.

Fun fact: the Southern Cross appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Samoa and Papua New Guinea.

name: Cygnus
description:
Cygnus, the Swan, is often said to be Zeus in disguise. Its bright stars form the Northern Cross.

Its brightest star, Deneb, is a supergiant tens of thousands of times more luminous than the Sun, marking the swan's tail and a corner of the Summer Triangle. Albireo, at the head, is a lovely gold and blue double star in a telescope.

Cygnus is best seen on summer and early autumn evenings, nearly overhead.

Fun fact: Cygnus X-1, the first object widely accepted as a black hole, lies here.

name: Delphinus
description:
Delphinus, the Dolphin, was sent by Poseidon to find the sea nymph Amphitrite, who had fled his proposal. The dolphin persuaded her to marry him and was rewarded with a place in the sky.

Its brightest stars are Rotanev and Sualocin. Read backwards, they spell Venator Nicolaus, the Latin name of an astronomer's assistant who sneakily named them after himself.

Delphinus is best seen on late summer evenings, in August and September.

Fun fact: though small, its diamond shape is easy to spot near Altair.

name: Dorado
description:
Dorado, the Dolphinfish, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s, after the mahi-mahi sailors saw chasing flying fish in tropical seas.

Its brightest star, Alpha Doradus, is about magnitude 3.3.

Dorado lies far south and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: it holds most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, and the giant Tarantula Nebula within it.

name: Draco
description:
Draco, the Dragon, is often identified with Ladon, the dragon that guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides until Heracles killed it.

Its brightest star is Eltanin, in the dragon's head. Thuban, in the tail, was the North Star about 4,700 years ago, when the Egyptian pyramids were built.

Draco is circumpolar from Canada, so it's up all year. It's highest on summer evenings.

Fun fact: the Cat's Eye Nebula, the glowing shell of a dying star, lies in Draco.

name: Equuleus
description:
Equuleus, the Little Horse, is the second smallest constellation. Some stories make it Celeris, a brother of Pegasus given to Castor by Hermes.

Its brightest star, Kitalpha, is about magnitude 3.9.

It's best seen on early autumn evenings, in September and October, next to Delphinus.

Fun fact: Ptolemy included it among his original 48 constellations in the 2nd century, even though it's so small and faint.

name: Eridanus
description:
Eridanus, the River, is where Phaethon fell after losing control of his father Helios's sun chariot and being struck down by Zeus.

Its brightest star, Achernar, at the river's far southern end, is one of the flattest stars known because it spins so fast.

From Canada you can see the northern part of the river winding south from near Orion on December and January evenings. Achernar itself never rises here.

Fun fact: Eridanus is the sixth largest constellation.

name: Fornax
description:
Fornax, the Furnace, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s after the chemical furnace used in experiments.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Fornacis, is about magnitude 3.8.

From southern Canada it sits low in the south on December evenings. From farther north it's very hard to see.

Fun fact: the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, one of the deepest images of the universe ever taken, looked at a tiny patch of Fornax and found about 10,000 galaxies.

name: Gemini
description:
Gemini, the Twins, are Castor and Pollux. When mortal Castor died, Pollux, who was immortal, asked to share his immortality with him, so Zeus placed them in the sky together.

Its brightest star is Pollux, an orange giant with a known planet. Castor is actually a system of six stars.

Gemini is best seen on winter evenings, high from January to March.

Fun fact: the Geminid meteor shower, one of the year's best, peaks every December.

name: Grus
description:
Grus, the Crane, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s. The crane was seen as a symbol of vigilance.

Its brightest star is Alnair, about magnitude 1.7.

From southern Canada only the northern edge of Grus rises, very low in the south on October evenings. Most of it never clears the horizon.

Fun fact: Grus holds the Grus Quartet, a group of four galaxies tugging on each other.

name: Hercules
description:
Hercules is the Greek hero Heracles, famous for his twelve labours. He's pictured upside down, kneeling, with one foot on the head of Draco.

Its brightest star is Kornephoros. Four stars form the "Keystone" at the centre of the figure.

Hercules is best seen on summer evenings, high overhead in June and July.

Fun fact: the Great Globular Cluster (M13), on one side of the Keystone, holds hundreds of thousands of stars. In 1974, astronomers beamed the Arecibo radio message toward it.

name: Horologium
description:
Horologium, the Pendulum Clock, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s in honour of the pendulum clock invented by Christiaan Huygens.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Horologii, is about magnitude 3.9.

Horologium lies far south. Only its northern tip peeks above the horizon from southern Canada on December evenings.

Fun fact: it holds the Horologium Supercluster, one of the largest known structures of galaxies.

name: Hydra
description:
Hydra, the Water Snake, is often linked to the many-headed monster Heracles killed. In another story, it's the snake the lying crow Corvus blamed.

Its brightest star is Alphard, "the solitary one", an orange giant alone in a dim part of the sky.

Hydra is best seen on spring evenings, stretching low across the southern sky from March to May.

Fun fact: Hydra is the largest constellation, stretching more than 100 degrees across the sky.

name: Hydrus
description:
Hydrus, the Lesser Water Snake, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s. It's not to be confused with the much larger Hydra.

Its brightest star, Beta Hydri, is a nearby star much like an older version of our Sun.

Hydrus lies near the south celestial pole and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: it sits between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, two satellite galaxies of the Milky Way.

name: Indus
description:
Indus, the Indian, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s. The figure is thought to represent an Indigenous person the Dutch explorers met on their voyages.

Its brightest star, Alpha Indi, is about magnitude 3.1.

Indus lies far south and is essentially hidden from Canada.

Fun fact: Epsilon Indi, one of the closest stars at about 12 light-years, has a giant planet and a pair of brown dwarfs.

name: Lacerta
description:
Lacerta, the Lizard, has no myth. Johannes Hevelius created it in the 1680s to fill a gap between Cygnus and Andromeda.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Lacertae, is about magnitude 3.8, and its zigzag of stars is easy to miss.

Lacerta is best seen on autumn evenings, high overhead from September to November.

Fun fact: BL Lacertae, first thought to be a variable star, turned out to be an active galaxy and gave its name to a whole class of them.

name: Leo
description:
Leo, the Lion, is the Nemean lion killed by Heracles as the first of his twelve labours. No weapon could pierce its tough hide.

Its brightest star, Regulus, marks the lion's heart. A backward question mark called the Sickle forms its head and mane, and Denebola marks the tail.

Leo is best seen on spring evenings, from March to May.

Fun fact: the Leonid meteor shower radiates from Leo each November and has produced spectacular meteor storms.

name: Leo Minor
description:
Leo Minor, the Little Lion, has no myth. Johannes Hevelius created it in the 1680s from faint stars between Leo and Ursa Major.

Its brightest star is Praecipua, about magnitude 3.8. Oddly, it has no star labelled Alpha.

Leo Minor is best seen on spring evenings, high in March and April.

Fun fact: it holds Hanny's Voorwerp, a strange glowing gas cloud discovered in 2007 by a Dutch schoolteacher volunteering for the Galaxy Zoo project.

name: Lepus
description:
Lepus, the Hare, crouches at Orion's feet, where the hunter's dog, Canis Major, chases it across the sky.

Its brightest star is Arneb, a yellow-white supergiant. R Leporis, "Hind's Crimson Star", is one of the reddest stars known.

Lepus is best seen low in the south on winter evenings, in January and February.

Fun fact: one story says hares once overran the island of Leros, so a hare was placed in the sky as a reminder that you can have too much of a good thing.

name: Libra
description:
Libra, the Scales, is the only zodiac constellation that isn't a living creature. It's often linked to Astraea, goddess of justice, represented by neighbouring Virgo.

Its brightest stars are Zubeneschamali and Zubenelgenubi, Arabic for "northern claw" and "southern claw", from when these stars were part of Scorpius.

Libra is best seen low in the south on early summer evenings, in June.

Fun fact: some observers describe Zubeneschamali as having a greenish tint, which would make it the only green-looking naked-eye star.

name: Lupus
description:
Lupus, the Wolf, was pictured by the ancient Greeks as an animal speared by Centaurus. It was only called a wolf later, in Renaissance times.

Its brightest star, Alpha Lupi, is a blue giant of about magnitude 2.3.

From southern Canada, the northern part of Lupus rises low in the south on June evenings. From farther north it stays hidden.

Fun fact: in 1006, the brightest supernova ever recorded appeared in Lupus. It may have been bright enough to read by at night.

name: Lynx
description:
Lynx has no myth. Johannes Hevelius created it in the 1680s and said you'd need the eyes of a lynx to see it, because its stars are so faint.

Its brightest star, Alpha Lyncis, is an orange giant of about magnitude 3.1.

Lynx is high in the north on winter and spring evenings, from January to April. From much of Canada, parts of it never set.

Fun fact: the globular cluster NGC 2419 in Lynx is so far away, about 300,000 light-years, that it's nicknamed the "Intergalactic Wanderer".

name: Lyra
description:
Lyra, the Lyre, is the harp of Orpheus, whose music could charm animals, trees and even stones. After his death, his lyre was placed in the sky.

Its brightest star, Vega, is the fifth brightest star in the night sky and a corner of the Summer Triangle. Epsilon Lyrae, the "Double Double", is a pair of double stars.

Lyra is best seen on summer evenings, nearly overhead in July and August.

Fun fact: about 12,000 years from now, Vega will be the North Star.

name: Mensa
description:
Mensa, the Table Mountain, is the only constellation named after a place on Earth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s after Table Mountain in Cape Town, where he mapped the southern sky.

It's the faintest constellation, with no star brighter than about magnitude 5.

Mensa lies near the south celestial pole and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: part of the Large Magellanic Cloud spills into Mensa, like the clouds that often cap the real Table Mountain.

name: Microscopium
description:
Microscopium, the Microscope, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s after the compound microscope.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Gamma Microscopii, is only about magnitude 4.7.

From southern Canada it rises low in the south on September evenings, below Capricornus. From farther north it's very hard to see.

Fun fact: AU Microscopii, a young red dwarf, has a dusty disc and at least two planets, making it a key target for studying how planets form.

name: Monoceros
description:
Monoceros, the Unicorn, was introduced by Petrus Plancius around 1612. Its stars lie in the Milky Way between Orion and Canis Minor.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Beta Monocerotis, is about magnitude 3.7 and is a beautiful triple star in a telescope.

Monoceros is best seen on winter evenings, in January and February, inside the Winter Triangle.

Fun fact: it holds the Rosette Nebula and the Cone Nebula, two well-known regions where stars are being born.

name: Musca
description:
Musca, the Fly, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s. It's the only insect among the 88 constellations.

Its brightest star, Alpha Muscae, is about magnitude 2.7.

Musca lies far south, just below the Southern Cross, and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: it was first called Apis, the Bee, before Lacaille's name, Musca, stuck.

name: Norma
description:
Norma, the Carpenter's Square, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s after the set square used by carpenters and draftsmen.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Gamma² Normae, is about magnitude 4.

Norma lies far south. Only its northern edge barely rises from the southernmost parts of Canada, so it's effectively out of view.

Fun fact: the Norma Cluster, near the Great Attractor, is part of a huge concentration of galaxies that pulls on the Milky Way and its neighbours.

name: Octans
description:
Octans, the Octant, is named after a navigation tool invented in the 1730s. Lacaille placed it at the south celestial pole in the 1750s.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Nu Octantis, is about magnitude 3.7.

Octans surrounds the south celestial pole, so it never rises from anywhere in Canada.

Fun fact: the southern pole star, Sigma Octantis, is barely visible to the naked eye, so southern navigators use the Southern Cross to find south instead.

name: Ophiuchus
description:
Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, is Asclepius, the healer who learned to raise the dead. Zeus struck him down, then placed him in the sky holding Serpens, the snake.

Its brightest star is Rasalhague, marking his head.

Ophiuchus is best seen on summer evenings, in the south in June and July.

Fun fact: the Sun passes through Ophiuchus each year from late November to mid-December, so it's sometimes called the 13th zodiac constellation. Barnard's Star, one of our nearest neighbours, is here too.

name: Orion
description:
Orion, the Hunter, was a giant hunter in Greek myth. In one story he boasted he could kill any animal, so Gaia sent a scorpion to kill him. They were placed on opposite sides of the sky, so Orion sets as Scorpius rises.

Its brightest stars are blue-white Rigel and the red supergiant Betelgeuse. Three stars in a row form his belt.

Orion is best seen on winter evenings, from December to March.

Fun fact: the Orion Nebula, below the belt, is a stellar nursery you can see with the naked eye.

name: Pavo
description:
Pavo, the Peacock, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s. In Greek myth the peacock was sacred to Hera, who placed the hundred eyes of the giant Argus on its tail.

Its brightest star, Peacock, is about magnitude 1.9.

Pavo lies far south and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: the star Peacock only got its name in the 1930s, when Britain's Royal Air Force needed names for the navigation stars in its almanac.

name: Pegasus
description:
Pegasus, the winged horse, sprang from the neck of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her. The hero Bellerophon later rode him to defeat the monster Chimera.

Its brightest star is Enif, the horse's nose. Three of its stars, with Alpheratz in Andromeda, form the Great Square of Pegasus.

Pegasus is best seen on autumn evenings, high in the south from September to November.

Fun fact: in 1995, 51 Pegasi became the first Sun-like star found to have a planet.

name: Perseus
description:
Perseus was the Greek hero who beheaded the Gorgon Medusa and rescued Andromeda from the sea monster Cetus.

Its brightest star is Mirfak. Algol, the "Demon Star", marks Medusa's head and dims noticeably every 2.9 days as a companion star passes in front of it.

Perseus is best seen on autumn and winter evenings, high in the northeast from November to January.

Fun fact: the Perseid meteor shower, one of the best of the year, peaks every August.

name: Phoenix
description:
Phoenix, the mythical bird reborn from its own ashes, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s.

Its brightest star, Ankaa, is an orange giant of about magnitude 2.4.

From southern Canada only the northern edge of Phoenix creeps above the southern horizon on November evenings. Most of it never rises.

Fun fact: the Phoenix Cluster is one of the most massive galaxy clusters known, and its central galaxy forms new stars at a remarkable rate.

name: Pictor
description:
Pictor, the Painter's Easel, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Pictoris, is about magnitude 3.2.

Pictor lies far south and never rises from most of Canada.

Fun fact: Beta Pictoris, a young star, is surrounded by a huge disc of dust and has two giant planets, giving astronomers a view of a planetary system in the making.

name: Pisces
description:
Pisces, the Fishes, are Aphrodite and her son Eros, who turned into fish and tied themselves together with a cord to escape the monster Typhon.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpherg, is only about magnitude 3.6. A ring of stars called the Circlet marks one of the fish.

Pisces is best seen on autumn evenings, in October and November, below the Great Square of Pegasus.

Fun fact: the Sun is in Pisces at the March equinox, which marks the start of spring in the north.

name: Piscis Austrinus
description:
Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish, was said by the ancients to be the parent of the two fish in Pisces. It's often drawn drinking water poured by Aquarius.

Its brightest star, Fomalhaut, is the 18th brightest star in the sky. It sits alone in a dim region, earning the nickname "the Lonely Star of Autumn".

Piscis Austrinus is best seen low in the south on autumn evenings, in September and October.

Fun fact: Fomalhaut is surrounded by a wide ring of dust.

name: Puppis
description:
Puppis, the Stern, was once part of Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, until Lacaille split it into three constellations in the 1750s.

Its brightest star, Naos, is one of the hottest and most massive stars visible to the naked eye.

From southern Canada the northern part of Puppis is low in the south on February evenings, below Canis Major.

Fun fact: Puppis has no stars labelled Alpha or Beta, because those letters went to stars in Carina when the ship was split.

name: Pyxis
description:
Pyxis, the Mariner's Compass, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s, placing it beside the stars of the old ship Argo Navis.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Pyxidis, is about magnitude 3.7.

From southern Canada it's low in the south on March and April evenings.

Fun fact: T Pyxidis is a recurrent nova that has erupted several times, most recently in 2011.

name: Reticulum
description:
Reticulum, the Reticle, is named after the crosshairs Lacaille used in his telescope eyepiece to measure star positions in the 1750s.

It's small. Its brightest star, Alpha Reticuli, is about magnitude 3.3.

Reticulum lies far south and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: Zeta Reticuli, a pair of Sun-like stars, became famous in UFO lore after the 1961 Betty and Barney Hill abduction story.

name: Sagitta
description:
Sagitta, the Arrow, is one of the ancient constellations. In one story, it's the arrow Heracles shot at the eagle tormenting Prometheus.

It's the third smallest constellation. Its brightest star, Gamma Sagittae, is about magnitude 3.5.

Sagitta is best seen on summer evenings, from July to September, inside the Summer Triangle.

Fun fact: despite its faint stars, its arrow shape is surprisingly easy to recognise.

name: Sagittarius
description:
Sagittarius, the Archer, is a centaur aiming his bow at the heart of Scorpius. He's often linked to Crotus, a satyr said to have invented archery.

Its brightest star is Kaus Australis. Its main stars form the Teapot, with the Milky Way rising like steam from its spout.

Sagittarius is best seen low in the south on summer evenings, in July and August.

Fun fact: the centre of our galaxy, with its supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*, lies in this direction.

name: Scorpius
description:
Scorpius, the Scorpion, was sent to kill Orion, the boastful hunter. The two were placed on opposite sides of the sky, so Orion sets as Scorpius rises.

Its brightest star, Antares, is a red supergiant so large it would swallow the orbit of Mars if it replaced the Sun. Its name means "rival of Mars".

Scorpius is best seen low in the south on summer evenings, in June and July. From northern Canada its curled tail stays below the horizon.

Fun fact: it holds M4, one of the nearest globular clusters.

name: Sculptor
description:
Sculptor, originally the Sculptor's Studio, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Sculptoris, is only about magnitude 4.3.

From southern Canada it's low in the south on November evenings, below Cetus.

Fun fact: the south galactic pole lies in Sculptor, so looking there you see out of the Milky Way's disc. The bright Sculptor Galaxy is one of the things beyond.

name: Scutum
description:
Scutum, the Shield, was created by Johannes Hevelius in 1684 to honour Polish king John III Sobieski after his victory at the Battle of Vienna. It's one of the few constellations named after a real person's emblem.

It's small. Its brightest star, Alpha Scuti, is about magnitude 3.9.

Scutum is best seen on summer evenings, in July and August, in a bright part of the Milky Way.

Fun fact: its Wild Duck Cluster (M11) looks like a flock of ducks in flight.

name: Serpens Cauda
description:
Serpens Cauda, the Serpent's Tail, is half of Serpens, the snake held by Ophiuchus. Serpens is the only constellation split in two, with Ophiuchus between its head and tail.

Its brightest star is Eta Serpentis, about magnitude 3.3.

Serpens Cauda is best seen on summer evenings, in July and August.

Fun fact: it holds the Eagle Nebula (M16), home of the "Pillars of Creation" photographed by Hubble.

name: Sextans
description:
Sextans, the Sextant, has no myth. Johannes Hevelius created it in the 1680s in honour of the sextant he used to measure star positions, which he lost in a fire in 1679.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Sextantis, is only about magnitude 4.5.

Sextans is best seen low in the south on spring evenings, in March and April, below Leo.

Fun fact: it holds the Spindle Galaxy (NGC 3115), a galaxy seen edge-on.

name: Taurus
description:
Taurus, the Bull, is Zeus in disguise. He became a white bull to carry off Europa, a Phoenician princess.

Its brightest star, Aldebaran, is an orange giant marking the bull's eye. Nearby are two famous star clusters, the Pleiades, or Seven Sisters, and the Hyades.

Taurus is best seen on winter evenings, from November to February.

Fun fact: the Crab Nebula is the remains of a supernova seen by Chinese astronomers in 1054. It was bright enough to see in daylight for weeks.

name: Telescopium
description:
Telescopium, the Telescope, has no myth. Lacaille named it in the 1750s after the telescope.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Alpha Telescopii, is about magnitude 3.5.

Telescopium lies far south. Only its northern edge barely clears the horizon from the southernmost parts of Canada, in July and August.

Fun fact: Lacaille first drew it much larger, borrowing stars from neighbouring constellations, but it was later trimmed back.

name: Triangulum
description:
Triangulum, the Triangle, is one of the ancient constellations. The Greeks saw its three stars as the Nile Delta or the island of Sicily.

Its brightest star is Beta Trianguli, about magnitude 3.0.

Triangulum is best seen on autumn evenings, from October to December, between Andromeda and Aries.

Fun fact: the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 3 million light-years away, is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye under very dark skies.

name: Triangulum Australe
description:
Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s. Its three stars are brighter than those of the northern Triangulum.

Its brightest star, Atria, is an orange giant of about magnitude 1.9.

Triangulum Australe lies far south and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: it sits in the Milky Way, close to Alpha Centauri.

name: Tucana
description:
Tucana, the Toucan, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s, after the colourful bird of South America.

Its brightest star, Alpha Tucanae, is about magnitude 2.9.

Tucana lies far south and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: it holds most of the Small Magellanic Cloud and 47 Tucanae, the second brightest globular cluster in the sky.

name: Ursa Major
description:
Ursa Major, the Great Bear, is the nymph Callisto. Zeus loved her, and the jealous Hera turned her into a bear, so Zeus placed her in the sky.

Its seven brightest stars form the Big Dipper. Dubhe and Merak, at the end of the bowl, point to Polaris. Alioth is its brightest star.

Ursa Major is circumpolar from Canada, visible all year, and highest on spring evenings.

Fun fact: in the handle, Mizar and its faint partner Alcor were once used as an eyesight test.

name: Ursa Minor
description:
Ursa Minor, the Little Bear, is often said to be Arcas, Callisto's son, placed in the sky beside his mother.

Its brightest star, Polaris, the North Star, sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole, so the whole sky seems to turn around it. Its stars form the Little Dipper.

Ursa Minor is circumpolar from Canada and visible every clear night of the year.

Fun fact: Polaris's height above the horizon roughly equals your latitude, so it's higher in Yellowknife than in Toronto.

name: Vela
description:
Vela, the Sails, was once part of Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, until Lacaille split it up in the 1750s.

Its brightest star, Gamma Velorum, is a system of hot, massive stars, including the brightest Wolf-Rayet star in the sky.

Vela lies far south. Only its northern edge rises, very low, from southern Canada on March evenings.

Fun fact: the Vela Pulsar, the spinning remains of an exploded star, flashes about 11 times a second.

name: Virgo
description:
Virgo, the Maiden, is usually linked to Demeter, goddess of the harvest, or her daughter Persephone. She's often shown holding an ear of wheat.

Its brightest star, Spica, "the ear of wheat", is a hot blue star. Virgo is the second largest constellation.

Virgo is best seen on spring evenings, from April to June.

Fun fact: it holds the Virgo Cluster, over a thousand galaxies about 54 million light-years away, including M87, whose black hole was the first ever photographed.

name: Volans
description:
Volans, the Flying Fish, was created by Keyser and de Houtman in the 1590s, after the fish that leap from tropical seas.

Its brightest star, Beta Volantis, is about magnitude 3.8.

Volans lies far south and never rises from Canada.

Fun fact: it was often drawn being chased by Dorado, the dolphinfish next to it.

name: Vulpecula
description:
Vulpecula, the Little Fox, has no myth. Johannes Hevelius created it in the 1680s, picturing a fox carrying a goose in its mouth.

It's faint. Its brightest star, Anser, whose name means "goose", is about magnitude 4.4.

Vulpecula is best seen on summer and early autumn evenings, from July to September, inside the Summer Triangle.

Fun fact: it holds the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), and the first pulsar was discovered here in 1967.
